parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Using a simple kinetic model of matter, describe the structure of a solid.

markscheme_points.text: particles / molecules are very close together / touching in a regular repeating pattern (lattice)
particles / molecules vibrate about fixed mean positions

hints: Hint 1: Picture the molecules in a solid compared to a liquid or gas - how close are they and how ordered is their arrangement?
Hint 2: Think about what type of motion is still possible if the molecules are held in fixed positions by strong bonds.
parts.proper_answer: Molecules are closely packed in a regular (lattice) arrangement with strong intermolecular forces. Molecules vibrate about fixed mean positions.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Close Packing and Order**
Think of a solid as many tiny balls packed tightly together in neat rows. The separation between neighbours is very small and the pattern is regular. This is why a solid has a fixed shape and volume and cannot be easily compressed.

Step 2: **Motion Allowed**
Because the forces between molecules are strong, they cannot move freely past each other. The only motion they have is to vibrate to and fro about a fixed mean position. As temperature rises the amplitude of vibration increases.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The specific latent heat of vaporisation is much greater than the specific latent heat of fusion for the same substance.
Explain this, in terms of the spacing of molecules.

markscheme_points.text: much greater increase in spacing of molecules for vaporisation compared with fusion (more work done against intermolecular forces)

hints: Hint 1: Compare how far apart molecules end up after melting (solid to liquid) with how far apart they end up after boiling (liquid to gas).
parts.proper_answer: Vaporisation requires complete separation of molecules from liquid to widely spaced gas, breaking almost all bonds, whereas fusion only partly increases separation with molecules still close. More work is done against intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Latent Heat Does**
During melting or boiling the temperature stays constant, so the supplied energy does not increase kinetic energy. It does work to pull molecules apart against attractive intermolecular forces, increasing potential energy.

Step 2: **Compare The Change In Spacing**
In fusion, solid changes to liquid. Molecules are still close together, so only some bonds are loosened. In vaporisation, liquid changes to gas. Molecules go from close together to very widely separated, so almost all bonds must be broken completely. That needs much more energy per unit mass.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Determine the temperature at which the substance melts.
hints: Hint 1: On a temperature-time graph, look for the first flat section where temperature stays constant while solid changes to liquid.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read The First Plateau**
A flat (horizontal) part means a change of state. The first flat part, at the start of heating, is melting (solid to liquid). The second long flat part at $65^{\circ}\text{C}$ is boiling. Reading the temperature axis for the first flat gives about $-100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The power of the heater is $150\text{ W}$.
Use data from Fig. 3.1 to calculate, in $\text{kJ kg}^{-1}$, the specific latent heat of vaporisation $L$ of the substance.
hints: Hint 1: Identify the long horizontal section at $65^{\circ}\text{C}$ on Fig. 3.1 - this is vaporisation. Read its start and end times to find how long boiling lasts.
Hint 2: Convert that time interval from minutes to seconds and think how to link heater power in watts to total thermal energy supplied.
Hint 3: Recall how total energy for a change of state is linked to mass and specific latent heat, then rearrange to find $L$ in $\text{J kg}^{-1}$ before converting to $\text{kJ kg}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: Time for vaporisation $= 8.5 - 3.0 = 5.5\text{ min} = 330\text{ s}$. $E = Pt = 150 \times 330 = 49500\text{ J}$. $L = E/m = 49500/0.045 = 1.1 \times 10^{6}\text{ J kg}^{-1} = 1100\text{ kJ kg}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find The Vaporisation Time**
The flat section at $65^{\circ}\text{C}$ is boiling. It starts at about $3.0\text{ min}$ and ends at about $8.5\text{ min}$. So $$\Delta t = 8.5 - 3.0 = 5.5\text{ min} = 5.5 \times 60 = 330\text{ s}$$ Remember to work in seconds because $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Calculate Energy Supplied**
The substance is perfectly insulated, so all heater energy goes into the substance. $$E = P \Delta t = 150 \times 330 = 49500\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Use Latent Heat Definition**
For a change of state at constant temperature: $$E = mL$$ so $$L = \frac{E}{m} = \frac{49500}{0.045} = 1.1 \times 10^{6}\text{ J kg}^{-1}$$ Convert to $\text{kJ kg}^{-1}$ by dividing by 1000: $$L = 1100\text{ kJ kg}^{-1}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Suggest what can be deduced from the fact that section $\mathbf{Q}$ on the graph is less steep than section $\mathbf{P}$.

markscheme_points.text: gas has a higher specific heat capacity (than liquid)

hints: Hint 1: Section P is heating of liquid and section Q is heating of gas. For the same power, what does a smaller temperature rise per minute tell you about energy needed per degree?
parts.proper_answer: The gas (section Q) has a greater specific heat capacity than the liquid (section P).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Steepness To Heat Capacity**
On a sloping section, temperature is rising, so $P\Delta t = mc\Delta T$. For the same heater power $P$, a less steep slope means a smaller $\Delta T$ in a given time, so more energy is needed for each $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ rise. Section P is liquid heating and Q is gas heating, so $c$ of the gas is larger than $c$ of the liquid.
